e.etymology: A German pet form of Helene and Magdalene, now a popular full name in Germany. In the US it sits beside Lenny and Lennie as a short, friendly girls' name.
namesakes: Leni Klum (model, daughter of Heidi Klum)
Leni Riefenstahl (German director of Nazi-era propaganda films)

e.etymology: For girls, a medieval French pet form of Marie, used in English since the Middle Ages. For boys it comes from the surname, often honoring the general Francis Marion; John Wayne was born Marion Morrison.
namesakes: Marion Cotillard (Oscar-winning French actress)
Marion Barry (longtime mayor of Washington, DC)
Marion Jones (sprinter stripped of her Olympic medals)

assoc.t: US towns and counties named for Gen. Francis Marion

e.etymology: From a surname for someone who lived by the River Trent in the English Midlands. The ancient Celtic river name is often read as trespasser, a river given to flooding. Trent is also short for Trenton.
namesakes: Trent Reznor (Nine Inch Nails frontman and film composer)

e.etymology: From the Spanish title of the Virgin Mary, María de las Mercedes, Our Lady of Mercies. The car was named in 1901 for Mercédès Jellinek, the daughter of an early Daimler dealer.
namesakes: Mercedes Ruehl (Oscar-winning actress in The Fisher King)

assoc.t: Mercedes-Benz, the German luxury car maker

e.note: Most Americans hear the luxury car first, though the car was named after a girl.

e.etymology: A spelling of Clark, an occupational surname from Old English clerc, a cleric or clerk. Its use for girls follows Clarke Griffin, the heroine of the TV series The 100.
namesakes: Clarke Griffin (heroine of the TV series The 100)
Arthur C. Clarke (author of 2001: A Space Odyssey)
Emilia Clarke (Game of Thrones actress)

assoc.t: Clarke Griffin, heroine of the CW series The 100

e.etymology: A recent American coinage, a spelling of Jaxton, which adds the -ton ending of Paxton and Braxton to Jax, itself short for Jaxon or Jackson.
From the Spanish city of Valencia, in Latin Valentia, strength or vigor. It is also a Spanish surname and the name of a popular juice orange.

assoc.t: Valencia, Spain's third-largest city
Valencia orange, the classic juice orange
Valencia, a community in Santa Clarita, California

e.etymology: In the US mostly a spelling of Mia or Mya. Miya is also a Japanese given name and surname, written with various characters; as a word, miya means shrine.
From Arabic Alya, loftiness or the heights, related to Ali and Aliyah. In Turkey it is a form of Aliye, and in Russia Alya is a pet name for Alina, Alexandra and similar names.
A respelling of Corbin, an English surname from Old French corbin, little crow or raven, at first a nickname for someone with raven-black hair.
A spelling of Lia or Leah. Lia is the Italian, Portuguese and Greek form of Leah, the wife of Jacob in Genesis, and is also short for names ending in -lia.
An English occupational surname for a scribe or bookbinder, or for a bleacher of cloth. Its long American life as a first name honors the educator Booker T. Washington.
namesakes: Booker T. Washington (educator and founder of Tuskegee Institute)
Cory Booker (US senator from New Jersey)
Devin Booker (NBA All-Star guard)

assoc.t: Booker T. Washington, educator and author
the Booker Prize, a leading award for English fiction

e.etymology: The German and Scandinavian form of the Roman family name Aemilius, possibly from Latin aemulus, rival. Emily and Emilia share the source. In the US it was most common in the 1880s, in immigrant families.
The feminine form of Martin, from Latin Martinus, belonging to Mars, the Roman god of war. Saint Martina was a 3rd-century Roman martyr.
namesakes: Martina Navratilova (tennis champion with 18 Grand Slam singles titles)
Martina McBride (country singer)
Martina Hingis (Swiss tennis champion)

assoc.t: Martina Navratilova, tennis champion

e.etymology: A modern spelling of Payton or Peyton, an English surname from a place name meaning the farm of a man called Paega.
A spelling of Journey, the English word, from Old French journee, a day's travel. Journey came into use as a girls' name around 2000.

assoc.t: sounds like Journey, the band of Don't Stop Believin'

e.etymology: A blend of Anne and Lise, a short form of Elisabeth, used in Scandinavia and, as Anneliese, in Germany.
From Bilal ibn Rabah, a freed Ethiopian slave who became a companion of the Prophet Muhammad and the first to call Muslims to prayer. The Arabic root means to moisten.
namesakes: Bilal ibn Rabah (companion of Muhammad and the first caller to prayer)

e.etymology: From the woodland plant. It joined the botanical names of the late 1800s, peaked in the US around 1900, and is returning with Ivy and Hazel.
namesakes: Fern Arable (the girl who saves Wilbur in Charlotte's Web)

assoc.t: fern, the leafy woodland plant
Fern, the farm girl in Charlotte's Web

e.etymology: A spelling of Amira, the feminine of Arabic amir, prince or commander. The double e shows the long vowel of the Arabic.
From Arabic yasir, well-off or living in ease. Yasir ibn Amir was among the earliest converts to Islam and one of its first martyrs.
namesakes: Yasser Arafat (longtime Palestinian leader, who spelled it Yasser)

e.etymology: A spelling of Zara, which arose as a form of Sarah, Hebrew for princess, and is also explained as Arabic zahra, flower.

assoc.t: Zara, the Spanish fast-fashion clothing chain

e.etymology: From Sanskrit asha, hope or wish, a common name in India. In East Africa Asha is a separate name, the Swahili form of Arabic Aisha, living.

assoc.t: Asha, heroine of Disney's 2023 film Wish

e.etymology: The original Greek form of Andrew, from aner, man, the name of the first apostle called by Jesus. It is the standard form in Germany, Scandinavia and Greece.

assoc.t: the San Andreas Fault in California

e.etymology: A modern American coinage that joins the Tay- of Taylor to the -len ending of Jaylen and Kaylen.
From Hebrew immanu el, God is with us, the name Isaiah gives a promised child and the Gospel of Matthew applies to Jesus. This spelling follows the Hebrew; Emmanuel follows the Greek.
namesakes: Immanuel Kant (German Enlightenment philosopher)

e.etymology: From the US state, whose name, coined in the 1700s, means land of the Indians. Most people think of the film hero Indiana Jones, who in the story took the name from the family dog.
namesakes: Indiana Jones (adventuring archaeologist played by Harrison Ford)

assoc.t: Indiana Jones, the whip-cracking film archaeologist
Indiana, the Midwestern US state

e.etymology: A spelling of Mya or Maya. Maya has several unrelated sources, among them the Greek goddess Maia, a Sanskrit word for illusion and a pet form of Maria.
From the rock band Led Zeppelin, named for the airships built by the German count Ferdinand von Zeppelin. His surname comes from Zepelin, a village in northern Germany.

assoc.t: Led Zeppelin, the 1970s hard rock band
zeppelin, a rigid airship like the Hindenburg

e.etymology: The Welsh form of Ambrose, from Greek ambrosios, immortal. In Welsh legend Merlin is Myrddin Emrys, and the BBC series Merlin used Emrys as the wizard's secret name.

assoc.t: Merlin, called Myrddin Emrys in Welsh legend

e.etymology: A 20th-century American blend of Janice, or Jan, and Vanessa.
A modern American name in the family of Amiyah, Amya and Amaya, or Mia with an A in front. It has no settled meaning of its own.
e.note: People will split between uh-MEE-uh and uh-MY-uh on sight.
